title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**0.title**
The Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana ("Discrimination of the Principles of Sāṃkhya"), composed by the illustrious Ṣimānanda.
**0.1**
This [work] is set forth by Ṣimānanda, son of Raghunandana, a resident of Iṣṭikāpura, foremost among the brāhmaṇas of Kānyakubja. // 1 //
**0.2**
Salutation to you, O great-souled Kapila, originator of the Sāṃkhya, the promoter of the true knowledge of the twenty-five {{tattva|ontological principle}}s. // 2 //
**0.3**
[A disciple asks:] "Overwhelmed as I am by the threefold suffering, how can there be peace for me here? Therefore instruct me, O treasury of compassion, in such a way that birth and the rest [of saṃsāra] may cease." // 3 //
**0.4**
Thus questioned, the sage—a treasury of compassion—spoke to the world-weary [disciple]: the twenty-five sūtras have been expounded by the great-souled ones. // 4 //
**0.5**
Some poets have composed [it] in verse, other poets have expounded [it]: that very real import of the Sāṃkhya teaching is here being discriminated—by the dull Ṣimānanda, [self-deprecatingly] called "a hundred-fold belly-filler" and the like. // 5 //
**Tats_1**
[Base sūtra:] The {{prakṛti|productive principle}}s are eight.
**Tats_1.c1**
[Commentary, verse:] {{prakṛti|primordial nature}}, intellect and {{ahaṃkāra|I-maker}}, the {{tanmātra|subtle element}}s, the eleven organs, and the [gross] elements—taken collectively, these are just twenty-four.
**Tats_1.c2**
Within these very [twenty-four], by the distinction of attribute and attribute-bearer, are included quality, action, and universal. And being-a-{{prakṛti|productive principle}} is the condition of being the material cause—directly or mediately—of every {{vikāra|modification}}. Its etymology is: "that of which the configuration, in the form of transformation, is preeminent (prakṛṣṭā)." And it has the form of the triad of substances—{{sattva|illuminating constituent}} and the rest—indicated by [their] state of equilibrium.
**Tats_1.c3**
And the state of equilibrium is the abiding—without mutual conflict—of [the constituents], which though [individually] of the placid, the turbulent, and the deluded forms, and though [each] of a non-aggregated character, [yet abide] together with their preponderances [as if] aggregated. By way of the generic [aspect] there is the status of a [subordinate] constituent; by way of preponderance there is dominance; by way of the particular [aspect] there is disequilibrium. Hence [equilibrium] is the uncombined state, free of any more-or-less—that is to say, the state in which nothing is [yet] an effect.
**Tats_1.c4**
But the [evolutes] beginning with {{buddhi / mahat|the great principle}}—being effect-[states] of sattva and the rest—are never in a non-effect state; thus they are excluded [from primordial prakṛti]. It was said that [the equilibrium] is [merely] "indicated" in order to establish prakṛti-hood even in the state of disequilibrium. {{prakṛti|Nature}} possesses the constituents sattva and the rest because it is not other than sattva and the rest. And so the sūtra: "sattva and the rest are not its [mere] attributes, since [prakṛti] is of their very nature"—[meaning] that sattva and the rest are the very essence of prakṛti, not attributes of prakṛti.
**Tats_1.c5**
For since every effect is accounted for by the {{guṇa|constituent strand}}s alone, it would be pointless to posit a prakṛti distinct from them; and because both the sūtra and the commentary state it thus.
**Tats_1.c6**
As for [the expressions] "the constituents of prakṛti"—like "the trees of the forest"—[these are] meant with reference to part and whole; and [the statement] "sattva, rajas, and tamas became the constituents of prakṛti" is not a declaration that sattva and the rest are effects of prakṛti—for that would conflict with the statement of the eternity of the guṇas; rather it refers to the effect-[states of] sattva and the rest that serve as the cause of the great principle.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_1.c7**
The creation of the great principle and the rest arises from the disequilibrium of the guṇas. And that [creation] is a transformation fit for the designation "sattva" etc.—endowed, through commingling with its own kind, with the resultant illumination and so forth that mark off [each] from the other constituents. Thus the designation "sattva" etc. belongs only to disequilibrium, as the {{śruti|revealed scripture}} declares: "In the beginning this [universe] was just darkness (tamas); it lay in the Supreme; impelled by the Supreme it moved to disequilibrium. By the perception of disequilibrium [arises] the form of rajas—that, indeed, is rajas declared [to be]. By the perception of disequilibrium [arises] the form of sattva."
**Tats_1.c8**
And the triad of sattva and the rest is of the very nature of sattva and the rest. Although the triad of sattva and the rest is substantial—since it possesses qualities such as pleasure, illumination, lightness, and serenity, since it undergoes conjunction and disjunction, and since it is non-inherent yet a material cause—nonetheless it is called by the word "{{guṇa|constituent}}" because it serves the {{puruṣa|Self}} and because it binds the puruṣa, just as the sense-organs and the like [are so called].
**Tats_1.c9**
The common saying that the guṇas have the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion [holds] by the distinction of attribute and attribute-bearer—just as the mind [is said] to have the nature of volition. Therein {{sattva|the bright constituent}}, though possessed of many attributes such as pleasure, serenity, and illumination, is said to be of the nature of pleasure on account of [pleasure's] preponderance. So too {{rajas|the active constituent}}, though possessed of many attributes such as pain, turbidity, and activity, is said to be of the nature of pain by preponderance. And so {{tamas|the dark constituent}}, though possessed of many attributes such as delusion, concealment, and obstruction, is said to be of the nature of delusion by preponderance.
**Tats_1.c10**
Sattva is "the being of what is good (sat)"; by predominance of virtue (dharma) it is the highest, the [finest] instrument for the puruṣa. By association with passion, rajas is intermediate. By association with the obscuring attribute of tamas, [tamas] is the lowest. Sattva and the rest have innumerable manifestations, because they transform at every instant; and their mutual similarity and dissimilarity, through attributes such as lightness, is innumerable—as per the sūtra.
**Tats_1.c11**
And because the creation of many puruṣas and the rest at one time is heard [in scripture, the guṇas must be many]; for if each were a single manifestation it would have to be all-pervading, and then, in the absence of variety of conjunction, there could be no infinite variety of effects; and because there would be no other substance to serve as their delimiter.
**Tats_1.c12**
Therefore sattva and the rest are simply innumerable; the statement of their being three [refers] only to the three differentiating limiting conditions—like the Vaiśeṣikas' statement of nine substances. And sattva and the rest are, as appropriate, of atomic or all-pervading magnitude; otherwise the statement that rajas is by nature mobile would be contradicted. Since it is fitting that the cause of ākāśa be all-pervading [but] if every causal substance were all-pervading, no delimitation of effects would be possible.
**Tats_1.c13**
[Verse:] That [primordial nature] is devoid of sound and touch, uncombined with form and the rest, possessed of the three guṇas, the womb of the world, beginningless, [itself the] source and dissolution [of all].

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_1.c14**
Because of statements such as this, prakṛti is not included among atoms and the like. [Objection:] "Even so, if prakṛti consists of many manifestations of sattva etc. common to both atomic and all-pervading [things], the established doctrines of its being undelimited, one, and inactive are undermined." [Reply:] No; for its being undelimited is asserted precisely in respect of its being prakṛti, i.e. a causal substance—just as smells [are said to be] pervasive of earth in respect of their smell-hood; and the established doctrine that prakṛti is all-pervading is justified precisely by the all-pervadingness of the prakṛtis such as ākāśa.
**Tats_1.c15**
Likewise, the meaning of the word "one" is just the absence of difference by way of difference of puruṣa and difference of creation; this is understood from the śruti "the unborn one" (ajām ekām). Likewise the meaning of the word "inactive" is just the absence of such operations as determination and self-conceit; otherwise the agitation of prakṛti spoken of by śruti and smṛti would be inexplicable.
**Tats_1.c16**
Here is the formal proof: the effect [consisting of] the great principle etc., which is of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, is an effect of a substance of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion—because it is of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion—like a couch [made from] cloth and other [pleasurable] effects. This is the proof for prakṛti. And among external things, pleasure and the rest are [perceived] as a kind of excellence—just as [we say] "the form of the pot"—as in the cognitions "sandalwood-pleasure," "woman-pleasure," and so forth. So much by way of indication.
**Tats_1.c17**
[Verse:] The {{avyakta|unmanifest}}, intellect, {{ahaṃkāra|I-maker}}, and the pentad of {{tanmātra|subtle element}}s—these are the eight productive principles, and seven of them attain to manifestation.
**Tats_1.c18**
[Verse:] And because they are born from unmanifest prakṛti they are [also] called "unmanifest things"; for they are not made manifest as pots and the like are manifested in the world.
**Tats_1.c19**
[Verse:] The unmanifest, prakṛti, māyā, {{pradhāna|the chief}}, brahman, the cause, the undifferentiated, the "flower of darkness," the field (kṣetra), that named "the imperishable"—
**Tats_1.c20**
[Verse:] these and "the manifold-natured" and other names the wise have sung of it. Because it is not made manifest by the sense-organs, it is called "unmanifest"; and because it is without beginning, middle, or end, being part-less, it is so [called].
**Tats_1.c21**
The śruti says just this: "Soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable, and likewise eternal, devoid of taste and smell, without beginning or middle, higher than the great [principle], stable—this the learned proclaim to be {{pradhāna|the chief}}."
**Tats_1.c22**
[Verse:] Therefore it is marker-less, subtle, and likewise of a productive nature, one, common [to all]; therein the effect belongs to no one [in particular], not so the others [i.e. the evolutes, which are particular].
**Tats_1.c23**
[Verse:] {{buddhi / mahat|Intellect}}, the great one, mind, Brahmā, thought, discernment, the unprecedented, wisdom, prosperity, steadfastness, knowledge, continuity, memory—[these too are its names].
**Tats_1.c24**
[Verse:] By [the term] "belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha" the name of the great intellect (mahat) is intimated. From the constituents being agitated the three Vedas were born.
**Tats_1.c25**
"One form, three gods—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara." Thus it is Viṣṇu who, in the primal creations, becomes the self-existent (svayambhū) lord.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_1.c26**
Here, because the great principle, through its three portions of sattva and the rest, is the limiting basis of the triad of deities, [the deities are] three through non-discrimination of it. "But from sattva-dominant {{pradhāna|primordial matter}} the great principle was born"—and, the great principle being predominant, determination (adhyavasāya) is its function. Of the inner-organ "tree"—consisting of the triad of intellect, I-maker, and mind—the great principle is the seed-state. This is stated in the Sāṃkhyasūtra: "This very great principle, transformed in part by admixture of rajas and tamas, becoming the limiting adjunct of individual souls, conjoined with demerit and the like, becomes even mean; through coloration by the great [sattva] it becomes the opposite."
**Tats_1.c27**
Since the great principle is of the nature of the three guṇas, in the state when the body is agitated by the embodied [self] in the form of Viṣṇu as Time, through the predominance of the limiting adjunct in the form of a constituent, in the [state of] non-discrimination there is the status of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. There: the great one, identifying with deep sleep, is Śiva, whose adjunct has the form of the effect of tamas; identifying with dream is Viṣṇu, whose adjunct is the effect of sattva; identifying with waking is Brahmā, whose adjunct is the effect of rajas. There, by the principle of inferring the aggregate [from the parts], since the collective is not other than the individual, even a gnat and the like is just Viṣṇu—such is the import.
**Tats_1.c28**
But creation proceeds only in the sequence beginning with the great principle, not in the sequence beginning with the elements. And this [is stated] in the Kūrma [Purāṇa]: "The {{ahaṃkāra|elemental I-maker}} (bhūtādi), undergoing modification, created mere sound; from it arose the cavity of ākāśa, characterized by sound."
**Tats_1.c29**
"And [the I-maker], modifying ākāśa, created mere touch; from it air (vāyu) arises, and touch is held to be its quality"—and so forth.
**Tats_1.c30**
[Objection:] "But if it is so, ākāśa and the rest are mere modifications [and not causes]." [Reply:] How [could that follow]? For it is stated in the Purāṇas and elsewhere that ākāśa and the rest are causes of the subtle elements such as touch [only] through the mere support of the I-maker.
**Tats_1.c31**
[Verse:] This [primordial matter] is not the {{puruṣa|Self}}; it is inert as a post. The intellect is determinative. The state of being {{pradhāna|the chief}} arose from the all-pervading [matter] presided over by the puruṣa.
**Tats_1.c32**
[Verse:] As is the power of consciousness, so is its functioning, mingled with sattva, [yet] of the nature of the rajas-constituent—because of the [doctrine of] threefold composition (trivṛtkaraṇa) from the śruti.
**Tats_1.c33**
[Verse:] Knowledge, virtue, dispassion, and lordliness—these arise from sattva; whereas non-lordliness, non-dispassion, demerit, and ignorance—
**Tats_1.c34**
[Verse:] these are to be known as [arising] from tamas. They are declared to be the [eightfold] divisions of the intellect. Knowledge is this awakening to the [true] principles; virtue is the observance of what is enjoined by śruti;
**Tats_1.c35**
[Verse:] dispassion is non-attachment to objects; lordliness is [the powers] beginning with aṇiman. By the very reverse of each, that tetrad becomes tāmasa [dark].
**Tats_1.c36**
[Verse:] By knowledge comes liberation; by virtue an upward course; by dispassion, absorption into the imperishable; by lordliness, an unobstructed course.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_1.c37**
[Verse:] Thus this eightfold power, named "intellect," has been explained; it is a modification of {{pradhāna|the chief}} and is itself the prakṛti [source] of the I-maker.
**Tats_1.c38**
[Verse:] [As] "root-prakṛti" and so forth it has been described by the poets. "The I-maker is one"—if there is a desire to know this, then reflect [as follows].
**Tats_1.c39**
[Verse:] That which makes the utterance "I" is remembered as self-conceit (abhimāna): "I touch," "I taste," "I am the master," "by me it was taken"—
**Tats_1.c40**
[Verse:] and so forth was the designation of that [I-maker]. Hear now its divisions: the modificatory (vaikārika), the energetic (taijasa), and the elemental (bhūtādi) with [its] inference,
**Tats_1.c41**
[Verse:] and without inference—these five are proclaimed as its divisions. The modificatory is sāttvika; the elemental is remembered as tāmasa;
**Tats_1.c42**
[Verse:] the energetic is to be known as rājasa. From it [comes] the pentad of subtle elements; from the sāttvika [I-maker] the group of eleven organs is born.
**Tats_1.c43**
[Verse:] The presiding deities, however, are also said [to arise] from the energetic [I-maker]. If [it be asked] "how can the very same [arise twice]?"—[the answer is] because of the cause [being] the threefold composition.
**Tats_1.c44**
[Verse:] This "sound-subtle-element"—only sound is apprehended [in it]; but its distinctions such as the acute accent or the niṣāda note are not apprehended.
**Tats_1.c45**
[Verse:] Just so the "touch-subtle-element"—only touch is apprehended; but its particulars such as cold or softness are not obtained.
**Tats_1.c46**
[Verse:] So too the "form-subtle-element," and likewise the "taste-subtle-element" and the "smell-subtle-element": in these no particular [distinction] is apprehended.
**Tats_1.c47**
[Verse:] The {{tanmātra|subtle element}}s, being non-particularized, are called the subtle elements; they are objects of enjoyment, [both] placid and terrible, and by nature atomic.
**Tats_1.c48**
[Verse:] By reason of their being productive in form, the productive principles are proclaimed eight in number.
**Tats_2**
[Base sūtra:] The {{vikāra / vikṛti|modification}}s are sixteen.
**Tats_2.c1**
[Verse:] The eleven organs and the five great elements—these are just the sixteen modifications, and they do not partake of being a productive principle.
**Tats_2.c2**
[Verse:] Ear, skin, the two eyes, tongue, nose—this is the [set of] organs of knowledge; voice, hands, anus, generative organ, and feet are held to be the organs of action.
**Tats_2.c3**
[Verse:] They perform their respective actions and [give rise to] knowledge, as is required. The mind is of both natures, having the form of volition and the rest.
**Tats_2.c4**
[Verse:] "Instruments," "organs (indriya)"—this stream [of evolutes] is made up of the modificatory [I-maker]; they are designated as "the fixed positions" and as "the sense-faculties (akṣas)."
**Tats_2.c5**
[Verse:] Earth, water, fire, and also air and ether—these are just the five great elements, by reason of their service such as supporting and the rest.
**Tats_2.c6**
[Verse:] Water, by way of cohesion, is of service to the four [other elements]; fire by way of cooking, air by way of conveyance.
**Tats_2.c7**
[Verse:] Earth, possessing the five qualities beginning with sound, is held to have five qualities; water is accompanied by [the qualities] beginning with sound but is devoid of smell;
**Tats_2.c8**
[Verse:] fire possesses sound, touch, and form; in air, again, [there are] sound and touch; and thus in ether there is sound alone.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_2.c9**
[Verse:] But they are not [merely] embodied forms; rather they are of particularized configurations. The modifications are proclaimed as threefold: the placid, the terrible, and the deluded.
**Tats_3**
[Base sūtra:] The {{puruṣa|Self}} [is the third great category].
**Tats_3.c1**
[Verse:] [Called puruṣa] from his lying within the city [of the body] (puri-śayana), from being the measure, from filling (pūraṇa), from abundant operation—he is beginningless, all-pervading, conscious, {{guṇa|constituent}}-less, supreme.
**Tats_3.c2**
[Verse:] [He is] the seer, the enjoyer, the {{kṣetrajña|knower of the field}}, stainless, of a non-productive nature, subtle, eternal, and indeed beginningless, without middle or end.
**Tats_3.c3**
[Verse:] "All is pervaded by him"—therefore he is all-pervading; and because he possesses the experience of pleasure he is conscious, and likewise constituent-less.
**Tats_3.c4**
[Verse:] Through the absence of the constituents sattva and the rest, he is "supreme," remembered by [the word] "supremacy." Through connection with visible prakṛti he is the seer; through experiencing he is the enjoyer.
**Tats_3.c5**
[Verse:] In the field he knows what pertains to the constituents; hence he is proclaimed "{{kṣetrajña|knower of the field}}." Through the absence of contact with the auspicious, inauspicious, and so on, he is held to be stainless.
**Tats_3.c6**
[Verse:] Because he is seedless and does not bring forth [offspring], he is of a non-productive nature. Through being part-less and supra-sensible he is subtle; eternal, because he is everlasting.
**Tats_3.c7**
[Verse:] Thus the Sāṃkhya {{puruṣa|Self}} has been expounded by the ancient sages. Living being (jīva), creature, person, self, puruṣa, worshipper, man,
**Tats_3.c8**
[Verse:] field-knower, imperishable, life-breath, "who-is-this?", the knower, the unborn—these are the names, in the Sāṃkhya, of what is termed the puruṣa.
**Tats_3.c9**
So [it is said]: "He who knows the twenty-five principles, in whatever stage of life he abides—shaven, with matted locks, or wearing a topknot—is liberated; herein is no doubt."
**Tats_3.c10**
[Verse:] Is this {{puruṣa|Self}}, who is beyond prakṛti, an agent or a non-agent? If he were the agent of auspicious and inauspicious [deeds], he would do them without the three functions [of the guṇas]. [And] if agency belongs to the constituents seen in the world, how can [the puruṣa] be the attribute-bearer [of agency]?
**Tats_3.c11**
[Verse:] Conformity [to discipline] arising from restraint, observance, [self-]sprinkling, and right reckoning; in the manifesting of the transformation [that is] knowledge and lordliness—this is the sāttvika function.
**Tats_3.c12**
[Verse:] Passion, anger, greed, slandering others, censure, [self-]satisfaction, harshness whether provoked or unprovoked—this is well known as the rajas-intellect.
**Tats_3.c13**
[Verse:] Madness, intoxication, dejection, godlessness, addiction to women, sleep, sloth, cruelty, and impurity—this is the tāmasa function.
**Tats_3.c14**
[Verse:] Having seen this triad of functions, [we conclude that] agency belongs to the constituents; and [hence] the puruṣa is established as a non-agent—this is held to be the [Sāṃkhya] settled doctrine ({{vivekajñāna|established conclusion}}).
**Tats_3.c15**
[Verse:] Through the distorted perception [born] of rajas and tamas, the unwise one—veiling his own self—holds these constituents of operative prakṛti [to be his own], [thinking] "I do this for myself," and so despises [the truth].

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_3.c16**
[Verse:] Incapable of [so much as] containing the tip of a hair within his belly, yet he thought, "all this was done by me"; he is to be regarded like a madman—such is [his] ignorance. O Fate! who [is more deluded] than one who fancies himself learned?
**Tats_3.c17**
This is stated in the Gītā [3.27]: "Actions are in every way performed by the constituents of prakṛti; [yet] one whose self is deluded by the I-maker thinks, 'I am the agent.'"
**Tats_3.c18**
[Gītā 13.31:] "Because he is beginningless and constituent-less, this imperishable supreme Self, though dwelling in the body, O son of Kuntī, neither acts nor is tainted."
**Tats_3.c19**
[Gītā 13.29:] "And he who always sees that actions are in every way performed by prakṛti alone, [and sees] the Self as a non-agent—he [truly] sees"—and so forth.
**Tats_3.c20**
[Verse:] Now consider whether the {{puruṣa|Self}} is one or many. From the diversity of [people's] mixed pleasure, pain, and delusion, of [their] pure births and deaths, the plurality of puruṣas is established; and [also] from the distinction of worlds, stages of life, and social orders.
**Tats_3.c21**
[Verse:] If the puruṣa were one, a collapse of intelligence would follow: when one was happy, all in turn would have to be happy; when one was in pain, all would have to be in pain.
**Tats_3.c22**
[Verse:] Therefore plurality is well established; many puruṣas are remembered. From the diversity of configuration, womb, disposition, association, and bodily division—[i.e.] from the plurality of subtle bodies ({{liṅgaśarīra|transmigrating body}})—the Sāṃkhya teachers, beginning with Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha, and Patañjali, describe the plurality of puruṣas.
**Tats_3.c23**
The teachers who uphold the Veda—Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, Vyāsa, and the rest—[hold] the Self to be one; and so the śruti [says]: "The {{puruṣa|Cosmic Person}} alone is all this, what has been and what is to be; he is also the lord of immortality, [the one] who grows beyond [all] through [other] nourishment. That alone is fire, that the sun, that the wind, and that the moon."
**Tats_3.c24**
[Śruti:] "That alone is the bright [seed], that is brahman, those are the waters, he is Prajāpati; that alone is the truth and the immortal, he is liberation, that is the supreme goal."
**Tats_3.c25**
[Śruti:] "That is the imperishable, that is the adorable [splendour] of Savitṛ, than which there is nothing higher nor other; than which there is nothing subtler nor greater."
**Tats_3.c26**
[Śruti:] "Like a tree, [or] like a pillar, the One stands fixed in heaven; by that {{puruṣa|Person}} this [all] is filled. On every side [it has] hands and feet, on every side eyes, heads, and faces."
**Tats_3.c27**
[Śruti:] "On every side having ears in the world, it abides enveloping all; appearing through the qualities of all the senses, [yet] devoid of all the senses."
**Tats_3.c28**
[Śruti:] "The lord of every creature, the great refuge of all; on every side [are] all beings—[it is] the Self of all, the source of all."
**Tats_3.c29**
[Śruti:] "That in which all dissolves, the sages know as brahman; for the one Self of beings alone is established in each and every being,
**Tats_3.c30**
[Śruti:] "and is seen as one and as manifold, like the moon [reflected] in water; for that one great Self dwells in all beings, moving and unmoving, by which all this is pervaded"—and so forth.
**Tats_4**
[Base sūtra:] The {{traiguṇya|triad of constituents}}.
**Tats_4.c1**
[Verse:] Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the {{guṇa|constituent}}s; "the state of the three guṇas" is the {{traiguṇya|triad}}. Serenity, lightness, attachment, [and] from [right] application affection, uprightness,

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_4.c2**
[Verse:] contentment, forbearance—[these constitute] the form of sattva, which directly brings pleasure. Grief, rigidity, hatred, torment, weariness, conceit in enjoyment—
**Tats_4.c3**
[Verse:] these are the manifold forms of rajas, bringers of much pain. Tamas, by name, [consists of] concealment and the rest, loathsomeness, obscuration, and the like,
**Tats_4.c4**
[Verse:] marked by wretchedness, heaviness, sleep and so on, heedlessness, and sloth—of the nature of delusion, endless. Thus the triad of constituents is declared. One should know sattva as illuminating, rajas as activating,
**Tats_4.c5**
[Verse:] and tamas as destroying [i.e. obstructing]. [This] is termed the "triad of constituents."
**Tats_5**
[Base sūtra:] {{saṃcara / pratisaṃcara|Evolution}} (saṃcara).
**Tats_5.c1**
[Verse:] That state of equilibrium of the constituents which is prakṛti—from it, by its own nature, through agitation by Time, comes disequilibrium; of old, in the field joined to the Supreme,
**Tats_5.c2**
[Verse:] [first] intellect [arose], and then the I-maker, threefold, was born; [then] the subtle elements, the organs, and the great elements—in [due] sequence.
**Tats_5.c3**
[Verse:] Origination just in this sequence is proclaimed [to be] "evolution" (saṃcara).
**Tats_6**
[Base sūtra:] {{saṃcara / pratisaṃcara|Involution}} (pratisaṃcara).
**Tats_6.c1**
[Verse:] In just the reverse order they dissolve: the pentad of [gross] elements [dissolves] into the subtle elements; the subtle elements and the organs dissolve into the I-maker;
**Tats_6.c2**
[Verse:] then the I-maker [dissolves] into the intellect, and the intellect into that named the unmanifest; [but] the unmanifest is dissolved into nothing. This is remembered as "involution" (pratisaṃcara).
**Tats_7**
[Base sūtra:] The subjective (adhyātma), the objective (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaivata).
**Tats_7.c1**
[Verse:] Intellect, I-maker, and mind; ear, skin, and the two eyes; likewise tongue, nose; feet, anus, and generative organ—[this] is termed the "subjective" (adhyātma).
**Tats_7.c2**
But as for [what is said] in the Mokṣadharma: "In the beginning the mind arises from the I-maker, and those [other] functions [too]. From craving for sound, the ear of this contemplating self arises; from craving for form, likewise the eye; the nose [arises] from the desire to grasp [and] conquer smell"—
**Tats_7.c3**
—by this and the like, the organs' being effects of craving [as a] function of mind and so forth is to be understood [as stated] only in accordance with the Vedānta method. [Now] the "objective" (adhibhūta):
**Tats_7.c4**
[Verse:] In due order: the to-be-cognized, the to-be-self-appropriated, the to-be-willed, the to-be-heard, the to-be-touched, and the to-be-seen,
**Tats_7.c5**
[Verse:] the to-be-tasted, the to-be-smelled, the to-be-gone-to, the to-be-emitted, and the to-be-delighted-in—thus is the "objective" proclaimed [as the set of objects of the organs].
**Tats_7.c6**
And the "divine" (adhidaivata): Brahmā, Rudra, the Moon, Ākāśa, and Vāyu, the Sun, Varuṇa, Indra, and likewise Viṣṇu and Mitra—
**Tats_7.c7**
—in just this order is the "divine" set forth. He who, as with an eye, comes to know the four [groups] in their own forms, or the divine [order]—freed from the taint of contact as it comes—enjoys the constituents but is not bound by the constituents.
**Tats_8**
[Base sūtra:] The five intellectual faculties (abhibuddhis).
**Tats_8.c1**
[Verse:] The {{buddhi / mahat|intellect}} is to be known through [its] inclinations, by its facing-toward action: "this is my task," "I do [it]"—this is determination (adhyavasāya).

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_8.c2**
[Verse:] Wish (icchā), longing (vāñchā), then volition (saṅkalpa), and the activity of the mind [i.e. self-conceit, abhimāna]—thus these five intellectual faculties are proclaimed.
**Tats_9**
[Base sūtra:] The five wombs of action (karmayonis).
**Tats_9.c1**
[Verse:] Steadfastness (dhṛti), faith (śraddhā), desire for pleasure (sukhecchā), the wish to know (vividiṣā), and the absence of that [wish to know]—these five, generally stated, are the wombs of action.
**Tats_9.c2**
[Verse:] That by which conviction in speech, in action, and in volition is colored [i.e. firmed]—being grounded in it and established upon it—this indeed is the mark of steadfastness (dhṛti).
**Tats_9.c3**
[Verse:] Freedom from envy, chastity, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifice, austerity, receiving [gifts], and oblation—[these] are remembered as the mark of faith (śraddhā).
**Tats_9.c4**
[Verse:] One who seeks pleasure would resort to pleasure: learning, [ritual] action, and austerities, ever devoted to expiation—this is proclaimed as "the pleasure[-seeking]" (sukhā / sukhecchā).
**Tats_9.c5**
[Verse:] Like one stupefied by poisonous smoke, the wish to know (vividiṣā) is the womb of wisdom for meditators—[knowing] both unity and separateness, the eternal [and] the unconscious [prakṛti as] knowable;
**Tats_9.c6**
[Verse:] that subtle, [already] existent effect which can be agitated [into manifestation] is to be known [as the object of] the wish to know; the wish to know, which makes [one] fit for [discerning] effect and instrument, is a function of prakṛti.
**Tats_9.c7**
[Verse:] Steadfastness, faith, the wish to know, and pleasure-[seeking]—this tetrad is to be known as bondage; [but] the wish to know is also ordained for liberation. Thus the nature of the wombs of action has been proclaimed in detail.
**Tats_10**
[Base sūtra:] The five vital airs (vāyus).
**Tats_10.c1**
[Verse:] Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—these are the five vital airs in the bodies of embodied beings.
**Tats_10.c2**
[Verse:] That which moves about the mouth and nose is called prāṇa, from [its] breathing (prāṇana); that which moves below the navel for the carrying-down is held to be apāna.
**Tats_10.c3**
[Verse:] From its location in and leading [of nourishment to] the heart it is proclaimed samāna; from its upward movement from the throat it is remembered as udāna.
**Tats_10.c4**
[Verse:] From its location in the joints, [and] from [its functions of] dispersing and stretching, [there is] vyāna.
**Tats_11**
[Base sūtra:] The five "action-selves" (karmātmans).
**Tats_11.c1**
[Verse:] The [five], beginning with the modificatory (vaikārika), have been set forth before in due order. [The permutations are:] the auspicious, the inauspicious-and-deluded, the auspicious-deluded, and the inauspicious-deluded—[these] in due order are the agents, [each] correlated with its respective deed.
**Tats_12**
[Base sūtra:] {{avidyā|Nescience}} of five joints (pañcaparvā avidyā).
**Tats_12.c1**
[Verse:] Darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra), and blinding gloom (andhatāmisra)—[these are the five joints of nescience].
**Tats_12.c2**
[Verse:] Those two—darkness and delusion—are each eightfold, grounded in the eight prakṛtis [taken as the self]. This [great delusion] is the self-conceit of [false] self-knowledge, the pride in the lordly powers beginning with attainment (prāpti);
**Tats_12.c3**
[Verse:] in regard to the five fulfilled objects—the seen [and] likewise the scripturally-heard—the delusion that is the conceit "I," which is the great delusion, is tenfold.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_12.c4**
[Verse:] In regard to the eight lordly powers and the ten objects, [the affliction] called "gloom" (tāmisra) is reckoned eighteenfold; the despair [at their loss], called "blinding gloom" (andhatāmisra), is met with at death.
**Tats_12.c5**
[Verse:] This nescience of five joints is divided into sixty-two varieties.
**Tats_13**
[Base sūtra:] Incapacity (aśakti) in twenty-eight ways.
**Tats_13.c1**
[Verse:] Dullness [of hearing], leprosy [of skin], blindness [of sight], [loss of] taste, [loss of] smell, dumbness, lameness, withered-arm, anal disorder, impotence, and madness—this [list of injuries to the organs] is thus set forth.
**Tats_13.c2**
[Verse:] The injury of the eleven organs—in the form of deafness and the rest—[gives eleven]; the injury of the intellect is seventeenfold, [consisting of] the inversions of the {{tuṣṭi / siddhi / aśakti|contentments and attainments}} [i.e. nine inverted contentments and eight inverted attainments].
**Tats_13.c3**
[Verse:] The conviction "there is no {{pradhāna|primordial nature}}" is [the inverted contentment called] "ajambhikā"; "there is no great principle" is [the inversion of] "salila"; and "āyācchā" [is inverted] in [the denial] "there is no I-maker";
**Tats_13.c4**
[Verse:] or "there is no unseen [merit]"—[the denial that] the pentad of subtle elements is the cause of the [gross] elements. "All this is just brahman; being brahman alone, one attains brahman"—as is the view of the Vedāntins, so [erroneously, here is held to be] such an opinion of [these false] Sāṃkhyas.
**Tats_13.c5**
[Verse:] Engagement in acquiring objects [is the inverted external contentment "asutā"]; engagement in safeguarding [them is] "sutarā"; engagement in [amassing] wealth by one who does not see the fault of acquisition [is] "asunetrā"—so it is proclaimed by the Sāṃkhyas.
**Tats_13.c6**
[Verse:] "Akurmarīcikā" is the capacity for enjoyment of one who does not see violence and the rest [as faults]; "anuttambhāmbhasikā" is the engagement in [worldly] water [i.e. activity] on account of the enjoyment of faults.
**Tats_13.c7**
[Verse:] These nine are declared to be the inversions of contentment. Now the eight attainments [in inversion] are stated; these are the inversions of the attainments:
**Tats_13.c8**
[Verse:] For one who reasons toward plurality, the establishing of the One is [the inverted attainment] "atāraka"; misapprehension from [mere] hearing of words is "asutāraka";
**Tats_13.c9**
[Verse:] Having heard "the knower of plurality is liberated," the knower of unity is not a sharer in liberation—[this is the inverted "tāra"]. Through entanglement in ignorance and bad scriptures that do not carry one across; and [the inverted] "apramodā" is, in transmigration, the absence of agitation even in one who suffers.
**Tats_13.c10**
[Verse:] "Apramuda," or that "apramodamāna" [which is being] gladdened by ignorance—[arising] either from incorrect instruction or from obstruction in regard to the teacher;
**Tats_13.c11**
[Verse:] for the unfortunate there would be no attainment in knowledge—so it is declared. "Aramyaka" is the [relapse into] ignorance after knowledge, through affectionate association [with the unworthy].
**Tats_13.c12**
[Verse:] These eight inversions of attainment have been explained in the foregoing manner. Thus incapacity in twenty-eight ways has been explained by the combination of both [the eleven organ-injuries and the seventeen intellect-injuries].
**Tats_14**
[Base sūtra:] {{tuṣṭi / siddhi / aśakti|Contentment}} (tuṣṭi) in nine ways.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_14.c1**
[Verse:] Having taken {{prakṛti|primordial nature}} itself to be the supreme Self, one becomes content; should one rest in [such] indifference, that contentment is called "ambhas"; and [taking] the intellect to be the supreme Self, that contentment is remembered as "salila."
**Tats_14.c2**
[Verse:] When it occurs in regard to the I-maker, it is termed "āyācchā"; when that contentment occurs in regard to the subtle elements, it is declared "dṛṣṭi" [vṛṣṭi].
**Tats_14.c3**
[Verse:] These four contentments arise as "internal" (ādhyātmika); yet in them too there is no liberation, [which comes] only from the knowledge of the [true] principles, as has been stated.
**Tats_14.c4**
[Verse:] "There is pain in acquiring objects, and in safeguarding what is acquired; pain in letting go, pain in their loss—fie on wealth, that vessel of pain!"
**Tats_14.c5**
[Verse:] [Thinking] "contented through seeing [these] faults, the supreme brahman alone is a sharer in liberation"—this is the fifth contentment, "sutā," [yet it too fails] through the absence of the knowledge of the [true] principles.
**Tats_14.c6**
[Verse:] The sixth is "sutarā," [contentment] in regard to safeguarding; the seventh, "sunetrā," from seeing [the fault of] their loss; and the eighth, "kurmarīcikā," [whose fault is] the fault of attachment;
**Tats_14.c7**
[Verse:] and desisting from [pursuit of] wealth because of the fault of violence and the rest—the ninth contentment, called "samaskarī" [uttamāmbhasikā], is the highest of these, [O disciple].
**Tats_15**
[Base sūtra:] {{tuṣṭi / siddhi / aśakti|Attainment}} (siddhi) in eight ways.
**Tats_15.c1**
[Verse:] The knowledge that arises [even] from afar [i.e. by reasoning] is the first, named "tārā"; knowledge of beings [arising] by mere [hearing of] words is held to be "sutārā";
**Tats_15.c2**
[Verse:] knowledge [arising] through study, which carries one across, is the third; from the removal of internal (adhyātmika) suffering it is called "pramodā";
**Tats_15.c3**
[Verse:] from the removal of elemental (ādhibhautika) affliction the attainment "pramuditā" is named; from the removal of divine (ādhidaivika) affliction, knowledge arises for men—
**Tats_15.c4**
[Verse:] the sixth attainment, of the virtuous, is called "pramodamānā"; from the cessation of [the fault of] affectionate association, the seventh is remembered as "ramyakā";
**Tats_15.c5**
[Verse:] and the eighth attainment, "pramudā" [sadāpramuditā], [arises] through service and the like to the teacher. Thus these eight attainments, which accomplish knowledge, have been explained.
**Tats_16**
[Base sūtra:] The ten radical topics (mūlikārthas).
**Tats_16.c1**
[Verse:] Existence [of prakṛti], oneness, purposefulness, being-for-another's-sake, otherness, non-agency [of puruṣa], conjunction, disjunction, the plurality of {{puruṣa|Selves}}, and the persistence of the body [as] residual operation (śeṣavṛtti)—[these are the ten].
**Tats_16.c2**
[Verse:] This is the enumeration of the ten radical topics. From the [composite's] being-for-another's-sake, the existence of {{puruṣa|the Self}} is established [as] the cause of the difference of transformation. "The unmanifest exists, [it is] infinite, one"—and being-for-another's-sake, [discerned] through the nature of love and despair [in beings] and [through their] manifold ruin, [establishes purposefulness]; likewise the establishment of [puruṣa's] otherness from the three-constituent [prakṛti].
**Tats_16.c3**
[Verse:] From the inversion [of agency onto prakṛti follows] the non-agency [of puruṣa]; conjunction [is] for the sake of the puruṣa's seeing; and when the dissolution of the body has been attained, [disjunction follows] from the perception that [prakṛti's] purpose has been accomplished.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_16.c4**
[Verse:] From the difference [in beings] of [everything] from birth down to the organs, they [i.e. the puruṣas] are remembered as many. The residual operation [of the body, persisting] like the spinning of a [potter's] wheel [after the impulse has ceased]—[thus] the ten radical topics are established.
**Tats_16.c5**
[Verse:] These fifty notions [the contentments, attainments, etc.] were taught before by the [Sāṃkhya]saptati. But with the ten [radical topics and the] sixty categories, [the system] is called the "Ṣaṣṭitantra" (the Sixty-Topic Treatise).
**Tats_17**
[Base sūtra:] The gracious creation (anugraha-sarga).
**Tats_17.c1**
[Verse:] Brahman created the gracious [creation] apart from the form-subtle-element, having produced [it] through the contemplation of grace, by abandoning the prior substrate.
**Tats_18**
[Base sūtra:] The creation of beings (bhūta-sarga) in fourteen kinds.
**Tats_18.c1**
[Verse:] Of eight varieties [is the divine creation]: the divine (daiva), the demonic (paiśāca), the rākṣasa, likewise the gandharva, the [realm] of Indra (aindra), the brāhma, the saumya, and the brāhmya—[these] eight.
**Tats_18.c2**
[Verse:] These are the divine wombs; but the animal (tiryak) womb is fivefold, distinguished as wild beast, [domestic] animal, bird, reptile, and the stationary [i.e. plants].
**Tats_18.c3**
[Verse:] And the human is of one kind, [ranging] from the brāhmaṇa down to the caṇḍāla. The [domestic] animals [range] from the cow down to the mouse; the birds [are those] beginning with Garuḍa,
**Tats_18.c4**
[Verse:] down to the gnat; the wild beasts [range] from the lion down to the jackal; the serpents [range] from Śeṣa down to the water-snake; [the stationary are] mountains, earth, and grasses,
**Tats_18.c5**
[Verse:] [these are] the stationary. [Such] is the creation of beings—this [is] the entire circle of transmigration (saṃsāra-maṇḍala).
**Tats_19**
[Base sūtra:] Bondage (bandha) is threefold.
**Tats_19.c1**
[Verse:] The {{prakṛti|nature}}-bondage is the absorption into prakṛti of one who conceives [it] as the supreme; the second, the modificatory (vaikārika) [bondage], is the absorption [of attention] of renunciants upon the organs;
**Tats_19.c2**
[Verse:] the sacrificial-fee (dakṣiṇā) bondage is of householders who pride themselves on [their] liberality. Thus this bondage is threefold; [and now] threefold liberation is declared.
**Tats_20**
[Base sūtra:] Liberation (mokṣa) is threefold.
**Tats_20.c1**
[Verse:] From the surge of knowledge and from cessation [of attachment] comes the destruction of merit and demerit; and from the destruction of merit and demerit comes what is sung [of] as {{kaivalya|absolute isolation}}.
**Tats_20.c2**
This is stated: "The first liberation is by knowledge, the second by the utter destruction of passion, and the third by the total destruction [of merit and demerit]. [Thus] the characteristic of liberation has been explained."
**Tats_21**
[Base sūtra:] The means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa) is threefold.
**Tats_21.c1**
[Verse:] The seen [perception], inference, and the word of a trustworthy person—this is [the threefold] means of valid knowledge. The five sense-organs [yield] perception; but [the inference of] rain [is made] by the rising of clouds—
**Tats_21.c2**
[Verse:] [this is] inference. "Indra [is] the king of the gods"—[such] verbal [testimony] is the means of cognition [i.e. trustworthy word].
**Tats_21.c3**
And in scripture (āgama) too: "Released from his own works, free of passion and hatred, possessed of knowledge, endowed with [good] conduct—such a one is to be known [as a trustworthy authority], and [the object] to be known is of like [trustworthiness]."

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**Tats_22**
[Base sūtra:] Suffering (duḥkha) is threefold.
**Tats_22.c1**
[Verse:] Suffering is declared threefold: the internal (adhyātmika), the elemental (adhibhautika), and the divine (ādhidaivika); and of these the first is remembered as twofold—
**Tats_22.c2**
[Verse:] bodily and mental, born of the disorders [of wind, bile, phlegm] and of desire and the rest. That which arises from beings—humans and the like—is the elemental (ādhibhautika).
**Tats_22.c3**
[Verse:] That which arises from the divine [powers]—cold, wind, and the rest—is the divine (ādhidaivika). This, in brief, is the commentary on the sūtras, [given] to the best of [my] understanding.
**Tats_22.c4**
[Verse:] And I shall [now] expound the systematic procedure (prakriyā), for the benefit of those [versed in] the Purāṇas.
**Tats_23**
[Base sūtra:] This [is] the truth [received] through [unbroken] tradition (paramparā).
**Tats_24**
[Base sūtra:] Having known all this, one becomes one whose task is accomplished (kṛtakṛtya).
**Tats_25**
[Base sūtra:] [And] one is no longer overcome by the threefold suffering. [These three sūtras carry no separate gloss; their substance is unfolded in the recapitulation that follows.]
**26.c1**
The great principle, the I-maker, and the five subtle elements are [also] termed "unmanifest"; by the word "great" (mahat) the {{buddhi / mahat|intellect}} of Hiraṇyagarbha is meant. {{pradhāna|The chief}}, the root, is termed "unmanifest." The knower (jña) is the {{puruṣa|Self}}. These are the twenty-five {{tattva|principles}}. Among them, {{pradhāna|primordial matter}} is cause only, never effect. The seven beginning with the great principle are effects of what precedes [each] and causes of what follows. The eleven organs and the five great elements are effects only, not causes.
**26.c2**
But the puruṣa is neither effect nor cause. This is stated [in the Sāṃkhyakārikā]: "root-prakṛti" and so forth. The great principle, the I-maker, and the five subtle elements—these seven are both productive and modified ({{vikāra / vikṛti|prakṛti-and-vikṛti}}). "From {{pradhāna|the chief}} intellect is born"—so [intellect] is a modification of the chief; "that very [intellect] generates the I-maker"—so it is [also] a productive principle. The I-maker too "is born from intellect"—so it is a modification; "it too generates the eleven organs and the five subtle elements"—so it is [also] a productive principle.
**26.c3**
Therein: "the sound-subtle-element is born from the I-maker"—so it is a modification; "from it ākāśa is born"—so the sound-subtle-element is a productive principle. Likewise "the touch-subtle-element is born from the I-maker"—a modification; "that very [element] generates air"—a productive principle. So too "the form-subtle-element is born from the I-maker"—a modification; "that very [element] generates fire"—a productive principle. "The taste-subtle-element is born from the I-maker"—a modification; "that very [element] generates water"—a productive principle. Likewise "the smell-subtle-element is born from the I-maker"—a modification; "that very [element] generates earth"—a productive principle.
**26.c4**
These five subtle elements, [being] the subtle elements, are the causes of the gross elements; and the group of sixteen is [pure] modification: five organs of knowledge, five organs of action, the eleventh being the mind, and five great elements—this group of sixteen is modification only, not productive principle. But the puruṣa is neither of the two—such is the meaning.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c5**
The means of valid knowledge is threefold, in the form of perception, inference, and word. Therein, perception is the pentad beginning with the ear, which grasps the worldly qualities such as sound; and inference grasps a non-perceived object [by a mark], such as smoke. Word, again, is of three kinds: the object of the vocal organ, the object of the ear, and the object of the intellect alone. Among these, the sound delimited by a place such as throat or palate is the object of the vocal organ, being its effect; and the sound that stands in the ear, mediated by the vocal organ—being sound [arising] from sound—is the object of the ear, being grasped by it. But words such as "pot" are the object of the intellect alone, since (by the reasoning to be stated) they are grasped by the intellect alone.
**26.c6**
Those words, precisely because they are the instrument of [conveying] meaning, are called {{sphoṭa|the word-whole}}. For that word is distinct from the individual phonemes uttered by the vocal organ; since, owing to the exceedingly swift perishing of the phonemes, there can be no combination [of them], the designation "a single word" could not become an object of usage, nor could [the phonemes] serve to recall the meaning [if there were no sphoṭa].
**26.c7**
And the cause of this {{sphoṭa|word-whole}} is a single particular effort [of articulation]; for if the utterance were [made] by [several] distinct efforts, there would be neither the usage "one word" nor the cognition of the meaning. And the manifester of this sphoṭa is the cognition of the final phoneme as qualified by the [proper] sequence; hence it is the intellect alone that grasps the sphoṭa, since grasping is possible only by the intellect through [grasping] the sequence—[and] by the relation of co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya-pratyāsatti) there is economy (lāghava) in [holding] the cognition of the sequence to be the cause of the manifestation of the word called sphoṭa.
**26.c8**
For just this reason the {{sphoṭa|word-whole}} cannot be grasped by the ear; for the sequence—being formless, as in "gha," then "ṭa," and so on—cannot be grasped by the ear, and the phonemes, perishing exceedingly swiftly, cannot be combined; and because it is fitting that it is the inner organ alone that cooperates [in this], since the impressions of the successive earlier phonemes and the recollections of them reside in the inner organ.
**26.c9**
[Objection:] "Granted all this; [but] let word-hood, or the capacity to convey meaning, belong to the very manifester of the sphoṭa—namely, the final phoneme as qualified by the sequence. Enough of [positing] the sphoṭa! By the maxim 'let that [property] belong to the very cause of that [effect].' This very [point] is stated by the Sāṃkhyasūtra: 'By [the alternatives of] being cognized and not being cognized, sound is not of the nature of sphoṭa.' The cognition of unity, too, is accounted for by the unity of the final phoneme as qualified by the sequence."
**26.c10**
To this it is replied: If so, the [doctrine of the] whole (avayavin) would have to be abolished [as well]. For [by your reasoning], since there is economy in positing that it is the parts alone—delimited by the particular conjunction that is the non-inherent cause—that cause the fetching of water and the like, by the parity of the same maxim "let that belong to the very cause of that," the cognitions "one pot" and the like would [also] be accounted for like the cognition "one forest" [which is merely a collective of trees, with no real whole].

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c11**
[Objection:] "The proof of the whole is this and the like: since atoms and their conjunctions are supra-sensible, if [the gross object] were of their nature [alone], the perception of the whole would be unaccountable [hence a whole over and above the parts must be admitted]." [Reply:] The same [argument] applies to the {{sphoṭa|word-whole}}: since the sequence is constituted of supra-sensible instants and the like, if the word were merely of the nature of the final phoneme as qualified by the sequence, the perception [of the word] would be unaccountable—this and the like is the proof of the sphoṭa.
**26.c12**
Moreover, we posit the sphoṭa-word on the authority of śruti alone, just like heaven and the like; hence, even in the absence of a worldly means of proof there, there is no defect.
**26.c13**
Thus: having declared that the three morae of the praṇava (Oṃ), in the forms a, u, and m, consist of the triad of deities beginning with Brahmā, the śrutis teach a fourth mora of the praṇava, consisting of the supreme brahman that transcends the triad of deities. That fourth mora can only be the {{sphoṭa|word-whole}}, distinct from the three phonemes; and it is called "the half-mora" (arddhamātrā): just as in an [undivided] heap, [so] of phoneme and word being undivided, the phonemes are one half and the word the other half—thus it is accounted for.
**26.c14**
And just as the whole cannot be dealt with [as] separated from its parts, so too the word cannot be uttered [as] separated from the individual phonemes. Hence it is remembered [in scripture]: "the half-mora abides, eternal, which is in particular not [separately] utterable."
**26.c15**
[Objection:] "Granted, the half-mora may be accounted for; but what is the nature of the [terms] nāda and bindu?" [Reply:] When the praṇava is uttered, the particular tone that arises—like the sound of a conch or a flute—is the nāda; and the exceedingly subtle state of the cessation of the nāda, being equivalent to the void, is called the bindu. Therefore, just as the whole is distinct from the parts, so the word is distinct from the phonemes, and that very [word] is the {{sphoṭa|word-whole}}—so it is established. [Objection:] "If so, a sentence too would be a sphoṭa." [Reply:] No [objection]—in the absence of a defeater, let it be accepted. So much by way of indication.
**26.c16**
Word (śabda), then, is characterized by the sentence of a [reliable] instructing person, such as "Indra [is] the king of the gods." If presumption (arthāpatti), [reasoning from] possibility, [from] non-existence (abhāva), tradition (aitihya), intuition (pratibhā), and comparison (upamāna) are means of valid knowledge, then they are to be subsumed here [under the three already stated], not [taken] separately. Though {{prakṛti|primordial nature}} and {{puruṣa|the Self}} exist, they are not perceived, owing to their subtlety—just as in the sky, smoke, vapour, mist, and atoms, though existing, are not perceived. By seeing the effect [consisting] of the great principle and the rest, {{pradhāna|the chief}} is inferred as its cause.
**26.c17**
The effect [consisting] of the great principle etc., produced from the three-constituent chief, is in part similar to prakṛti [the cause] and in part similar to the modification—since in the world the effect in the form of a son is seen [to be] of both sorts. And that effect is existent (sat), not non-existent, not [both] existent-and-non-existent, not inexpressible; for in [case of] utter non-existence, oil would arise even from sand-grains, and the other two positions are simply self-contradictory. {{pradhāna|The chief}}, termed "unmanifest," is independent, all-pervading, and eternal; the effect, termed "manifest," is dependent, non-pervading, and non-eternal. The puruṣa is independent, all-pervading, and eternal.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c18**
{{pradhāna|The chief}} is the cause of the three worlds, and it is one, by economy [of explanation]. At the time of dissolution, the effect [consisting] of the great principle etc. dissolves into the chief. And that chief consists of sattva, rajas, and tamas. {{prakṛti|Nature}} is the state of equilibrium of the three constituents. The chief is unconscious, but the {{puruṣa|Self}} is conscious—distinct from both the manifest and the chief, pure, devoid of constituents. Since the effect generates pleasure, pain, and delusion, the sattva, rajas, and tamas that are its cause therein are to be inferred.
**26.c19**
And it is observed, respectively, that a passionate woman generates pleasure, pain, and delusion in [her] husband, [her] co-wife, and a paramour. So too in the three-constituent effect: when, on account of [a person's] unseen [merit], sattva becomes preponderant, then, overpowering rajas and tamas, it generates its own effect, pleasure. Likewise when rajas becomes preponderant, then, overpowering sattva and tamas, it generates its own effect, pain. And when tamas becomes preponderant, then, overpowering sattva and rajas, it generates its own effect, delusion.
**26.c20**
Suffering is threefold, by the distinction of internal, elemental, and divine. To explain: therein, the internal is of two forms, bodily and mental. The bodily, then, is fever, dysentery, and the like, caused by disorder of wind, bile, and phlegm; the mental is that born of separation from the dear, union with the undesired, and so forth. The elemental is occasioned by the fourfold class of beings: it arises from animals, birds, beasts, humans, reptiles, gnats, lice, bedbugs, and stationary [beings]—[that is,] from the womb-born, egg-born, sweat-born, and sprout-born. That which arises from heaven (dyu) is "divine"; what is produced with reference to it is the divine [suffering], born of cold, heat, wind, rain, and the fall of thunderbolts.
**26.c21**
As assembled threads [produce] a cloth, so {{pradhāna|the chief}}, consisting of an aggregate of constituents, generates the effect [consisting] of the great principle etc. And just as water from the sky, though of one taste, on falling into a pond and the like comes to have another taste through contact with the pond etc., so too, from the single-formed chief, gods and the rest become, in turn, happy, suffering, and utterly deluded.
**26.c22**
Thus, through the predominance of sattva and the indifference of rajas and tamas, the gods are utterly happy; through the predominance of rajas and the indifference of sattva and tamas, humans are utterly suffering; through the predominance of tamas and the indifference of sattva and rajas, animals are utterly deluded. The aggregate [consisting] of the great principle etc. presupposes an enjoyer, because it is an object of enjoyment, like a couch. The aggregate [consisting] of the great principle etc. is dependent on another, because it is unconscious, like a garland. Thus the {{puruṣa|Self}} is inferred. And it is many, because of the difference, for each [individual], of births, deaths, and organs.
**26.c23**
This is the meaning: if there were but one Self, then at the death of one, all would die; at the birth of one, all would be born; at the defect of one's organs, all would have defective organs. But it is not so observed; therefore [the Self is] many. From correct knowledge whose sphere is the twenty-five principles, the {{kaivalya|isolation}} of the puruṣa comes about. And that [is] "otherness"—that is to say, [the puruṣa's] difference from {{pradhāna|the chief}} and the rest.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c24**
From non-discrimination [comes] transmigration; from discrimination, {{kaivalya|isolation}}. In effect, [this amounts to] acceptance of the doctrine of non-apprehension (akhyāti-vāda). For this very reason the cognition "this is silver" is not [an] error, but rather a pair of cognitions undistinguished both in their own form and in [their] object. The conclusion is: for whomever the object of the silver-cognition "this is silver" is of such-and-such a kind, the world is for him just of that kind.
**26.c25**
For this very reason, transformation (pariṇāma)—as characterized by the definition "the real, essential becoming-otherwise of a thing"—is accepted [for prakṛti, not for puruṣa]. And that {{puruṣa|Self}} is not many, one per body, because it is unchanging. In truth it is a non-agent, indifferent like one liberated, like a witness. Sattva, rajas, and tamas are [both] agents and [the deeds] done. Though a non-agent, the puruṣa is treated [in common usage] as if an agent—just as a non-thief, seized along with thieves, [is treated as] a thief. Because [it is] not distinct from the constituents, prakṛti is the agent, not the puruṣa.
**26.c26**
The puruṣa, which has the power of seeing [but] is devoid of the power of action, [enters into] conjunction with {{pradhāna|the chief}} in order to see the chief, [in all its extent] down to the great principle, the [other] elements, and so on. And the chief, which is devoid of the power of seeing [but] has the power of action, [enters into] conjunction with the puruṣa for the sake of [its] liberation; when, through the distinctness of the puruṣa, knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the puruṣa has arisen, the liberation of the chief comes about [i.e. it ceases to act].
**26.c27**
[Objection:] "Liberation is the experience of eternal bliss." [Reply:] [That is] unsound, since experience too is caught up in the discrimination of eternal and non-eternal. Nor can one say that the human goal is just the breaking of some veil—of nescience and the like—over [an experience] whose sphere is eternal bliss; for [then] the experience of bliss itself would be the human goal, and because, consciousness being eternal, even a veil [over it] is impossible. As for the śruti and smṛti [passages speaking] of supreme bliss in liberation, they are merely the conventional idiom of the scriptures on liberation.
**26.c28**
[Verse:] "There is only suffering, no pleasure—since it [pleasure] is [merely] apprehended [as] the relief of one tormented by suffering, [where] the designation 'pleasure' is applied. Suffering is the craving for sensual pleasure; pleasure is remembered as [merely] the passing-away of suffering."
**26.c29**
By such smṛti [passages], the cessation of suffering alone is conventionally [termed] "pleasure." The Sāṃkhyasūtra too [says]: "the cessation of suffering is [only] secondary," and "the praise of release [as bliss] is for the dull-witted." The attainment of bliss is a secondary liberation that occurs in the world of brahman; thereafter, when both {{pradhāna|the chief}} and the puruṣa have accomplished their purpose, their disjunction occurs, like the [parting of the] union of the blind man and the lame man.
**26.c30**
To explain: one was lame and the other blind. Both, travelling on a dangerous road with a great caravan, were by fate abandoned by their kinsmen; lacking respectively the power of movement and the power of sight, they joined together for the sake of [the one] seeing and [the other] moving. So the lame man was mounted on the shoulder of the blind man, and the blind man walks by the path shown by him, while the lame man walks [too], being mounted on the blind man's shoulder. Afterwards, once each has reached his own country, having accomplished their purpose, they part.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c31**
And so {{pradhāna|the chief}}, having brought about the liberation of the puruṣa, desists. The puruṣa neither engages nor desists. The puruṣa is the seer and the enjoyer; enjoyment is characterized by [its] terminating in consciousness, not [by its] consisting in absorption in action. And that puruṣa transmigrates through beginningless non-discrimination; through hearing the true scriptures and the grace of a teacher, free of doubt, when {{vivekajñāna|discriminative knowledge}} has arisen, it is liberated. From the conjunction of prakṛti and puruṣa, transmigration is produced.
**26.c32**
As a child [is born] from the union of woman and man, so the great principle is born from prakṛti. From the great principle the I-maker is born; and it is threefold—modificatory (vaikārika), elemental (bhūtādi), and energetic (taijasa). The modificatory is the sāttvika; the elemental is the tāmasa; the energetic is the rājasa. Therein, from the modificatory I-maker the eleven organs and their presiding deities are born; from the elemental I-maker the subtle elements are born; from the energetic I-maker [both] the group of eleven organs and the pentad of subtle elements are born.
**26.c33**
[Objection:] "Since these two groups are respectively born from the modificatory and the elemental I-maker, how can [their] re-origination [from the energetic] be spoken of?" If [you ask] this, then hear.
**26.c34**
When, overpowering rajas and tamas, the sattva-constituent becomes preponderant, [and] the I-maker—receiving the name "modificatory," [being] of an inactive nature—taking the energetic I-maker as its helper, generates the eleven organs that are of an active nature, then those [organs], availing themselves of the pretext of [the energetic's] assistance, are said to be made by the energetic [I-maker] in its own form as well.
**26.c35**
And when, overpowering sattva and rajas, the elemental [I-maker], in which the tamas-constituent is preponderant, taking the form of the energetic I-maker as its helper, makes the pentad of subtle elements active in nature, then that pentad of subtle elements is said to be made by the energetic too, by its very assistance; from that active pentad of subtle elements the pentad of [gross] elements arises. This is the sequence of transformation: from the modificatory [come] the eleven organs, [and] from the elemental the pentad of subtle elements.
**26.c36**
This is the meaning: in the generation, respectively, of the two effects—the modificatory's and the elemental's, each active in nature—there is the assistance of the energetic I-maker; and it is precisely from the energetic I-maker's rendering of assistance that the effect characterized by these two groups is active in nature. The organs that generate cognition are the organs of knowledge: the organs of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin; and their objects are form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. "They perform action"—so [they are called] organs of action: voice, hands, feet, anus, and generative organ; and their objects are speech, taking, going, excretion, and delight.
**26.c37**
The mind is [both] an organ of knowledge and an organ of action, since it [forms the] volition for the functioning both of the organs of knowledge and of the organs of action; hence the mind is of both natures. The mind too is all-pervading, since it is the substrate of the latent impressions of merit and demerit; the inner organ, one per {{puruṣa|Self}}, is eternal, like ākāśa. Nor can one say that the unseen [merit] and the rest are simply attributes of prakṛti [in general]; for [then] there would be the over-extension [absurdity] that the unseen [merit] etc. residing in one [person] would produce pleasure, pain, and so on in another.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c38**
And it [the inner organ] cannot be atomic; for then the simultaneous direct intuition of everything, in its full extent, by yogins would be impossible. Nor can it be said that for yogins the relation [to objects] is just the merit born of yoga; for when [intuition] is accounted for by the ordinary relations—conjunction, inherence in what is conjoined, and so forth—there is no warrant for positing another mode of contact, [and there would be] prolixity (gaurava) and mutual deviation. And in positing a sub-class within the [several kinds of] direct intuition, [there would be] confusion of classes and excessive prolixity.
**26.c39**
In the yogic view, what is brought about by the merit born of yoga and the rest is merely the breaking of the veil called tamas over the inner organ, [which is itself] capable of grasping all objects—since it is established that in deep sleep tamas obstructs [its] functioning. Nor can the inner organ be of merely intermediate magnitude, for [then], being destroyed at dissolution, it could not serve as the substrate of the unseen [merit] etc. Hence, by elimination, the inner organ is established as just all-pervading. This is stated:
**26.c40**
[Verse:] "The mind-ether (cittākāśa), the consciousness-ether (cidākāśa), and the [physical] ether as the third—know the consciousness-ether to be the most void of the [other] two, O fair-faced one."
**26.c41**
[Objection:] "Granted this; [yet] even if, given the all-pervadingness of the inner organ, the obtaining of a delimited operation is accounted for by the veil, [its] going to other worlds and the like is not accounted for. For this very reason the Sāṃkhyasūtra [says]: 'the mind is not all-pervading, because it is an instrument,' or 'because of the scripture [speaking] of its going.' Moreover, if so, then by economy it would be more fitting to posit a veil over consciousness alone; for what purpose is an all-pervading inner organ posited, [only] for a veil obstructing knowledge to be posited over it?"
**26.c42**
To this it is replied: The scripture [speaking] of going is accounted for—as in the case of the Self, so too in the case of the inner organ—through the limiting adjunct of the breath, the organs, and so on, [and] from the duality of the inner organ as cause-form and effect-form. The going of the effect-inner-organ is accounted for even of itself; and the duality of the inner organ as cause-form and effect-form must be accepted by the Sāṃkhyas too, since otherwise—if [the inner organ] were effect only—the Sāṃkhyasūtra '[the qualities] beginning with merit are attributes of the inner organ' would be inexplicable,
**26.c43**
and—if [it were] eternal only—the sūtra [speaking] of the origination of the great principle and the rest would be inexplicable. As for the claim that it is fitting to posit a veil over consciousness alone—that is not fitting; for over immutable (kūṭastha) consciousness a veil in the form of an obstruction to knowledge is impossible. Nor can it be said that the very connection of consciousness with an object is to be posited as the obstruction, in the form of a reflection and the like; for even so the seeing of the Self would be unaccountable, since without the channel of an organ, the connection of [consciousness] with itself, in the form of a reflection and the like in itself, is impossible.
**26.c44**
Moreover, the inner organ being established as the substrate of wish, volition, and so on, the pots and the like seen internally in dream and the like are also posited as its transformations, since it is fitting that cause and effect be co-referential. And thus [the inner organ], transformed into the shapes of pots etc., appears in consciousness, [and] precisely through non-separation from that, the external pot and the like appears; hence a veil that obstructs just such a transformation is fitting there [in the inner organ]. Furthermore, by the observation of the veiling of the external organ, the inner veil too is inferred to reside in the organ; and the unveiled-ness of the Self [is established] by śruti and smṛti.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c45**
[Objection:] "Given the all-pervadingness of the inner organ, how can it be an effect?" [Reply:] No [difficulty]; for just as all-pervading ether-prakṛti has [as effect] the delimited transformation in the form of effect-ether, so too the inner-organ-prakṛti, through admixture with another constituent, has the delimited transformation in the form of the [effect-]inner-organ; and this is accepted on the authority of śruti and smṛti. So much by way of indication.
**26.c46**
The object of the mind is volition. These eleven [organs] are born from the modificatory I-maker—so it was said. The {{puruṣa|Self}} apprehends the object reflected in the intellect. This is stated: "the puruṣa is conscious of the object present in the intellect; 'I shall perform [my] duty'—[such] determination is the mark of the intellect. Virtue, knowledge, dispassion, lordliness—this [tetrad belongs] to the sāttvika intellect; the opposite—non-dispassion and the rest—is tāmasa."
**26.c47**
The world is pervaded by just the twenty-five principles, neither fewer nor more. Just as the [flow of] milk is for the sake of the calf's nourishment, so too the activity of {{pradhāna|the chief}}, [though] unconscious, is altogether fitting for the sake of the liberation of the {{puruṣa|Self}}.
**26.c48**
The {{liṅgaśarīra|subtle body}}, however, is the aggregate of eighteen—intellect, I-maker, mind, the [five] organs of knowledge, the [five] organs of action, and the five subtle elements. Within the twenty-three principles, excluding the five [gross] elements, and merging the I-maker into the intellect, the [resulting] seventeen[-fold aggregate] is termed the subtle body, since, like fuel for fire, it is the locus of the manifestation of the Self.
**26.c49**
And that [subtle body], having arisen at the beginning of creation for all puruṣas, persists until the dissolution of prakṛti; and it is by it alone that the transmigration of living beings here in this world and the next occurs. The breath (prāṇa) is but a distinct function of the intellect, and so is not specified separately from the subtle body. And the five subtle elements are the support of that subtle body—like [the wall is the support] of a painting—since, without a support, the exceedingly subtle [body] could not go to other worlds.
**26.c50**
And this {{liṅgaśarīra|subtle body}} arises first as one alone, [serving] as the limiting adjunct of the Self-existent (svayambhū)—like his gross body, called the Cosmic Form (virāṭ), to be described [below]. From it, then, the individual subtle bodies—the limiting adjuncts of individual souls, being portions of it—are divided off, like a son's subtle body from a father's subtle body. This is stated by the author of the sūtras: "distinction of individuals [arises] from distinction of action." And it is stated by Manu too [1.16]:
**26.c51**
[Manu 1.16:] "Having placed the subtle parts of these six [organs] of immeasurable power into [his own] self-portions, he fashioned all beings."
**26.c52**
"Of the six" means the six organs [the five plus the mind], which stands for the entire subtle body. And so the meaning is: the Self-existent, having joined the subtle, minute parts of his own subtle body into [his] self-portions—the conscious portions of himself—created all living beings. [So much for] the subtle body.
**26.c53**
As for the origination of the gross body: within the tenfold-multiplied great principle [arises] the I-maker; within that, tenfold-multiplied, [arises] ether (vyoman); within that, tenfold-multiplied, [arises] air; within air, tenfold-multiplied, [arises] fire; within fire, tenfold-multiplied, [arises] water; within water, tenfold-multiplied, earth arises—and that very [earth] is the seed of the gross body. That same earth-form seed is transformed into the form of an egg; and within that egg-form, tenfold-multiplied, earth-envelope, the gross body of the Self-existent, consisting of the fourteen worlds, arises from his mere volition. By that very body the Self-existent is called {{liṅgaśarīra|Nārāyaṇa}}.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c54**
This is stated by Manu [1.8] with reference to the Self-existent: "He, contemplating, desiring to create manifold beings from his own body, first created just the waters, [and] cast [his] seed into them."
**26.c55**
[Manu 1.9–11:] "That [seed] became a golden egg, radiant as the sun of a thousand rays; in it Brahmā himself was born, the grandsire of all the worlds. He, indeed, is the first embodied one; he is called the {{puruṣa|Person}}; the first agent of beings, Brahmā, came to be at the beginning."
**26.c56**
[Manu 1.10:] "The waters are called 'nārā,' for the waters are the offspring of Nara; since they were his first abode (ayana), he is therefore remembered as 'Nārāyaṇa'"—and so forth.
**26.c57**
And precisely because the individual puruṣas are divided off from that primal {{puruṣa|Person}}, and because at the end they dissolve back into that very [one], he alone is spoken of in śruti and smṛti as "the one Self." Hence, [this being meant] by way of [conventional] usage, there is no contradiction with the śruti and smṛti [passages] such as "Nārāyaṇa alone is the Self of all beings."
**26.c58**
And so that Nārāyaṇa, possessed of the Cosmic Form (virāṭ), having created upon Sumeru—which occupies the place of the pericarp of the lotus of his navel—the Self-existent called the Four-faced [Brahmā], by means of him created also the other individual embodied beings, down to the stationary [ones]. This is stated:
**26.c59**
"Together with those effects and causes arisen from his body, the {{kṣetrajña|field-knowers}} were born from the limbs of that wise one."
**26.c60**
As for what is heard—that the Four-faced [Brahmā] manifests from the navel-lotus, ears, eyes, and so on of Nārāyaṇa who reclines on Śeṣa—that is to be understood [as occurring] only in the daily creations, by the distinction of cosmic ages (kalpas). For it is only in the daily dissolutions that the gods, having entered and become one with the body of Nārāyaṇa and slept, manifest [again] from him who reclines on Śeṣa, in the sequence beginning with the Four-faced—not in the primal creations; for [his] reclining, in a sportive embodiment, [occurs] only in the daily dissolution.
**26.c61**
Thus, in brief, the twenty-four principles, their creation and dissolution, and [their] purpose have been stated. Therein, whatever arises from whatever, its persistence is precisely by the replenishing [from that source]; and therefore its dissolution too occurs into that very [source]. And so [it is said] in the Bhārata:
**26.c62**
[Mahābhārata:] "Whatever principle arises from whatever, that dissolves back into it; [the principles] dissolve in reverse order and arise in forward [successive] order."
**26.c63**
And these transformations of the twenty-four principles—in the form of creation, persistence, and dissolution—[being] gross, have been displayed for the sake of discriminating the immutable {{puruṣa|Self}}. Other, subtle [transformations] of theirs, [occurring] at every instant, are also remembered:
**26.c64**
[Verse:] "The constituent parts [of things], constantly being consumed [and renewed], come to be and cease to be by Time, whose velocity is imperceptible; owing to [their] subtlety, this is not apprehended."
**26.c65**
Hence every insentient thing is, in the highest sense, declared to be always non-existent [as an abiding entity]. And therefore, becoming dispassionate toward it, the {{puruṣa|Self}} alone, which is real in the highest sense, is to be beheld by those who fear suffering. This is stated:

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c66**
[Verse:] "Sprung from the seed of the unmanifest, made of the trunk that is the intellect, the great [tree], whose boughs are the great I-maker, whose hollows are the sprouting organs,
**26.c67**
[Verse:] whose main branches are the great elements and whose lesser branches are the particulars, ever-leafed, ever-blossoming, bearing the rise of auspicious and inauspicious fruit,
**26.c68**
[Verse:] the livelihood of all beings—[this is] the eternal brahman-tree. And having truly known this, and having [cut it] with the supreme sword of knowledge, [and] attaining imperishability, one abandons death and birth."
**26.c69**
This is stated: "The organs and the objects of the organs do not, indeed, [any longer] approach [him]; and the embodied one, bereft of [his] organs, no longer merits a [new] body. Therefore, from all-pervading passion (rāga) all creatures are born."
**26.c70**
Even in the absence of particular passion in hell and the like, because general passion is present, passion is the co-operating factor [with] action.
