In the [scriptural passage], with regard to the commencement of the poison-shaped [bondage], "that very attached [subtle body] goes along with [its] action"—[and] "the marker (liṅga) is the mind, to which [the soul] is attached"—it is established in the śruti that it is general attachment, called the latent impression of objects, born of self-conceit, passion, hatred, and so on, that is the co-operating factor in the poison-shaped commencement of birth and the rest.
**26.c71**
From the smṛti: "Upon whatever the embodied one fixes [his] mind entirely with [his] thought—whether from affection, from hatred, or even from [its] quality—he attains conformity to that very [thing]."
**26.c72**
[Verse:] "This one, his senses turned [inward], awakened by the mirror that is the teacher, clearly perceived the modification [of prakṛti] as other than himself, unstable, [imposed on him] through delusion.
**26.c73**
[Verse:] Then [thinking], 'I am not this prakṛti, for this is of a turbid nature; I am of a pure, awakened nature'—knowing thus, he abandons it.
**26.c74**
[Verse:] Thus, when the Self is recollected as pure [and distinct] from body, organs, and so on, this whole [prakṛti] with its modifications is virtually cast off, like a [shed] skin." [The reading 'tyak taprāyā' is to be corrected to 'tyaktaprāyā'.]
**26.c75**
[Objection:] "The {{avidyā|nescience}} that has the form of the cognition of [the] Self in the non-Self—how can it be destroyed by discriminative knowledge whose qualificand is the Self, given the difference of mode and so forth [between them]?" [Reply:] No; for such nescience is destroyed by the discrimination whose qualificand is the Self, by way of the discrimination whose qualificand is the non-Self.
**26.c76**
And the non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka) knowledge of the Self that arises through yoga becomes a cause of liberation only by way of {{vivekajñāna|discriminative knowledge}}, not directly—because it does not [itself] remove nescience. For it is the cognition "I am fair, an agent, happy, suffering," and the like, that is nescience—established by śruti, smṛti, and reasoning to be the cause of the calamity of transmigration; and what removes it is precisely the {{vivekakhyāti|discriminative discernment}} of the form "I am not fair," and the like—since, [the two having] the same object, there is opposition [only] by way of [the latter's] being a cognition of the absence of the grasped, qualified by the mode "absence of the grasped." Otherwise, even the non-conceptual [knowledge] of one liberated would have to be opposed to the cognition "this is silver."

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c77**
Furthermore, since opposition to the cognition of the grasped is necessarily [present] in the aforesaid cognition of absence, the power of non-conceptual cognition to remove error is not posited separately, [as that would entail] prolixity.
**26.c78**
Moreover, by the śruti "Now therefore the instruction: not thus, not thus (neti neti)... for there is nothing higher than this 'not thus'... [there is no] other supreme [reality]," and so on, it is declared that there is no teaching higher than the teaching of discrimination.
**26.c79**
[Gītā 13.34:] "Those who thus know, with the eye of knowledge, the difference between the field and the {{kṣetrajña|knower of the field}}, and the liberation of beings from prakṛti—they go to the supreme."
**26.c80**
—and by these Gītā statements it is declared that {{vivekajñāna|discriminative knowledge}} alone is the cause of liberation. Hence discriminative knowledge alone, by [its] direct removal of nescience, is the cause of liberation.
**26.c81**
But the direct intuition of the isolated Self [attained] through yoga brings about the apprehension of the absence of the attributes belonging to the limiting adjuncts and the difference [of the Self] from those adjuncts, by way of the [yogic] non-apprehension of what is fit [to be apprehended]; and from that [follows] the removal of nescience. By this [it is shown that] the knowledge of equality in all beings, and the knowledge of the Self's being the Self of all, and the like—sung of in śruti and smṛti—are, in all the systems, to be regarded as ancillary to discriminative knowledge alone.
**26.c82**
—since the other [forms of] knowledge do not directly remove self-conceit. In the Brahma-mīmāṃsā [Vedānta], however, this is the distinction: that [they] are ancillary to the discrimination of the supreme Self; whereas in the Sāṃkhya teaching [they] are ancillary to the discrimination of the [individual] Self in general. So much by way of indication.
**26.c83**
But the {{vivekakhyāti|discriminative discernment}} simply destroys nescience; it is not [merely] an obstruction [that allows] error to recur, as in the case of one who sees the discrimination of shell from silver—[for in that worldly case] error is revived through the abundance of faults such as cataract, desire, and so on [in the illustration]. And here, in the conceit of [the] Self in the non-Self, the fault is just the beginningless latent impression, agreed upon by all the orthodox—since in the conceit of one just born no other fault is apprehended. When that latent impression of false knowledge is uprooted by the firm impression produced by the succession of discriminative discernments, then alone is one said to be established in the direct intuition of discrimination. Before that, necessarily, through a trace of the latent impression, some portion of falsity still appears in the Self; but once that establishment in discriminative discernment has arisen, self-conceit can no longer occur, because the fault called the latent impression is [now] absent.
**26.c84**
If, however, the mutual reflection of intellect and {{puruṣa|Self}}, and the like, is held to be the fault [that is] the cause of non-discrimination, then the direct intuition of discrimination arises precisely by sublating that fault; hence it is not [again] a cause of error—for, on the strength of [its] result, that [fault] can be posited as a fault only when unaccompanied by the merit born of yoga.
**26.c85**
Although the grasping of discrimination in the form of the ultimate particular of the entities that are the counter-correlates of discrimination is not possible, nevertheless, because the general grasping of discrimination is possible by way of [shared characters such as] being-an-object-of-sight and being-subject-to-transformation, even in the absence of qualified [particular] knowledge of the entities such as prakṛti, {{vivekakhyāti|discriminative discernment}} in general is the cause of liberation. This is stated:

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c86**
[Verse:] "As the seer of a pot is [in every way] distinct from the pot, [being] in no way the pot, so the seer of the body is the embodied one—[discriminated] in the form 'I am not [the body],' and so on."
**26.c87**
As for [the śruti] "the Self, verily, is to be seen,"—here there is no [genuine] visibility of the Self; for although [the Self may be] pervaded by [a mental] function, it is not pervaded by [it] in the form of [being] a result. As for what is said even by the Buddhists—that the intellect, [though] experienced as possessing pleasure, pain, and so on, being self-luminous, is not pervaded by consciousness, just as the Vedāntins [say that] the Self, though experienced as "I," is not pervaded by the result called consciousness—that, being without proof, is to be disregarded.
**26.c88**
That [embodied being] arises in the creation [proceeding] from {{pradhāna|the chief}} and the rest. By the force of demerit it transmigrates among animals and the like; by the force of merit, among gods and the like. Precisely through non-knowledge of the [true] principles, [the subtle body,] tinged by merit and demerit, dissolves into the chief at the time of dissolution. Although the chief and the puruṣa are [both] all-pervading, it is prakṛti alone that effects the arrangement of the {{liṅgaśarīra|subtle body}}.
**26.c89**
The subtle body, augmented by the subtle atoms [and] the subtle elements, abides among humans and the like, like an actor: just as an actor, though one in his own form, takes on various forms by [changes of] costume, so the subtle body, entering within the womb, becomes an elephant, a woman, a man; [and likewise] there comes about the fivefold inversion (viparyaya) named darkness, delusion, great delusion, gloom, and blinding gloom.
**26.c90**
By merit [comes] the attainment of the higher worlds, such as that of Prajāpati; by demerit, the attainment of animals and the like; by ignorance, bondage; by the knowledge of the twenty-five principles, final release (apavarga). And that knowledge of the [true] principles, of such a kind, arises through hearing the scriptures from a teacher. To explain: distinct from {{pradhāna|the chief}} is the {{puruṣa|Self}}; distinct [from it] is the intellect, distinct the I-maker, distinct the subtle elements, the organs, and the five great elements.
**26.c91**
Every effect, though of the nature of the three constituents, is, with reference to the preponderant constituent, designated by the words "sāttvika" and so on. The conscious puruṣa, in the various wombs, is conscious of—i.e. experiences—the suffering wrought by old age and death; such is the meaning. So long as the {{liṅgaśarīra|subtle body}} is not made to cease by the knowledge of the [true] principles, so long does a new gross body arise and perish at each birth.
**26.c92**
Even in the absence of any purpose of its own, {{pradhāna|the chief}}—like a good friend, indifferent to any return of favour—undertakes the effect, [extending] from the great principle down to the [gross] elemental objects, for the {{puruṣa|Self}}'s enjoyment and liberation. {{prakṛti|Nature}}, having shown the intellect, the I-maker, and the rest [to be] distinct from the puruṣa, desists.
**26.c93**
Just as a dancing-girl, having shown to the audience the [performances] set to song and the like, with the [aesthetic] sentiments such as the erotic and the emotional states such as the comic, withdraws, her purpose accomplished—so too [is prakṛti]. Furthermore, prakṛti, [though] possessed of constituents, rendering service to the constituent-less {{puruṣa|Self}} who renders no service [in return]—by way of being the womb of the world, of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion, or by way of being the object [such as] sound and the rest, [and] by such services—afterwards reveals herself, [saying as it were] "I am other, you are other," and withdraws, like a good friend [who] desires no return of favour from the Self.

title: Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana
text:
**26.c94**
Of creation, neither God (Īśvara) is the cause, nor [mere] nature (svabhāva), nor Time (kāla). Even Time, for the yogins, is of the nature of the instant (kṣaṇa) alone—not, as for the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas, partless, eternal, and one like the Self, [posited] for [the sake of] economy. That very [instant], being delimited by this or that limiting adjunct, generates the usage [of temporal units] from the instant and the minute (muhūrta) up to the year. There is no separate category named "the instant."
**26.c95**
By the Sāṃkhyas it is laid down in the sūtra "space and time [arise] from ākāśa and the rest"; [hence] they hold that there is no separate category of Great Time (mahākāla) or instant and the like, but rather that ākāśa itself, qualified by limiting adjuncts, generates the usage [ranging] from the instant up to Great Time.
**26.c96**
But the yogin says that both these views are unsatisfactory; for by any [single] stable limiting adjunct, the usage of "the instant" is impossible [whether] from Great Time or from ākāśa. To explain: as the limiting adjunct for the instant-nature of Great Time or ākāśa, others hold the action of an atom and the like, delimited by conjunction with a posterior region, or some such other thing. To this it is said: if [the adjunct is] the action qualified by conjunction and the like—[then, being] merely the qualificand, the qualifier, and their relation—since the three are admitted by others to be stable, the usage of "the instant" is not possible by them.
**26.c97**
And if [the instant] is held to be something over and above those, [then] that is not Great Time or ākāśa; for, the usage of "the instant" being accounted for by that very [over-and-above instant], it would be pointless to posit that something else delimited by it is the cause of the usage of "the instant." And that instant, [being] unstable from [its] being qualified and so forth, is an exceedingly perishable particular transformation of prakṛti alone; hence there is no consequence of [its] being something over and above prakṛti and puruṣa.
**26.c98**
It is by particular accumulations of that very instant that the usage [of the units] beginning with the minute and the day-and-night, up to the [period of] two parārdhas, comes about; there is no partless Great Time, for there is no proof [of it]. The usage "today" and the like [is brought about] by the accumulation of instants alone; and the śruti and smṛti [passages speaking] of the eternity of Time refer to the eternity of the stream [of instants]. Therefore, by necessity, Time is of the nature of the instant alone; there is no partless Great Time, nor is ākāśa the cause of the usage of Time—rather, it is {{pradhāna|the chief}}.
**26.c99**
The {{puruṣa|Self}} is neither bound, nor liberated, nor does it transmigrate; rather, it is {{prakṛti|nature}} alone, having various substrates, that is so [bound, liberated, and transmigrating]. Thus all is consistent.
**26.colophon**
Thus is completed the Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana, composed by the illustrious Ṣimānandadīkṣita of Kānyakubja.
